chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Faddal, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
Standing at Al-Mash'ar is an obligation (fard), and standing at Arafah is a sunnah.

This does not contradict what we mentioned, because the meaning in this report is that its obligation was known from the side of the Sunnah, rather than from the explicit text of the Quran. And whatever its obligation is known from the side of the Sunnah, it is permissible to call it by the name of 'Sunnah'. We have explained this in other places.
But it is not so for standing at Al-Mash'ar, because its obligation is known from the explicit text of the Quran.
So when you depart from Arafat, remember Allah at Al-Mash'ar Al-Haram.

Thus He obligated upon us remembrance at Al-Mash'ar. And there was no command in the explicit text of the Quran regarding standing at Arafat, so for that reason it was attributed to the Sunnah. And this also indicates the obligation of standing at Arafat.

key_terms.سُنَّةٌ: Sunnah (tradition/practice, here used for non-explicit obligation)

ai.seo_question: Why is standing at Arafat considered Sunnah while standing at Al-Mash'ar is considered Fard in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi elucidates the jurisprudential nuance that while standing at Arafat is obligatory (wajib), it is classified as 'Sunnah' because its proof is derived from the Sunnah rather than an explicit Quranic verse, whereas standing at Al-Mash'ar is explicitly mandated by the Quran. This distinction highlights the Shia scholarly method of differentiating between the source of evidence (Quran vs. Sunnah) and the resulting legal ruling, demonstrating that a practice can be obligatory yet still bear the name of the Sunnah when its primary textual basis is prophetic tradition.
